articles.title: Social Security's latest COLA may fall short for retirees. Here's why.
articles.summary: The Social Security Administration announced the largest COLA since 2023, but experts say it may not be enough to keep pace with rising costs.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027.

It's the largest increase since 2023 and among the top 20 largest adjustments since 1975. But senior advocates say this raise is coming too late and won't be enough to help retirees keep up with the pressure of rising costs.

The Senior Citizens League's executive director, Shannon Benton, says seniors will find themselves disappointed when they look up the COLA announcement.

"When inflation spikes due to a geopolitical event like the Iran war, seniors pay the price. Prices go up today, but benefits stay the same for months due to an outdated COLA methodology," Benton said in a statement. "Working people can request a raise or seek a higher-paying position, but seniors have to make lifestyle cuts or drain their savings until the next COLA."

How much more retirees will get, and why advocates say it may not be enough

The Social Security Administration says the increase will add about $75 a month to retirees' monthly benefit payments, boosting the average payment from $2,087.52 to $2,162.67.

The problem, experts note, is that the COLA adjustment calculation is usually a little late to the game.

The Social Security COLA is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W, which tracks changes in the price of goods and services based on the spending habits of working households rather than retirees. It compares average CPI-W figures for July, August, and September with the same period a year ago to determine the appropriate benefit adjustment.

Once that adjustment is determined, beneficiaries won't see it reflected in their monthly payments until the start of the following year. In that time, prices can continue to rise, leading to a perpetual cycle of adjustments that fail to have a meaningful impact.

The adjustment is "supposed to offset inflation, but it under-measures it," Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance's Kerry Hannon, citing the war in Iran and tariffs driving costs higher. Read more about the math behind the hike .

According to TSCL's 2026 Senior Survey , 89% of respondents said the 2026 COLA was too low and felt their benefits would fall behind inflation.

"Congress cannot control every price increase, but it can act to ensure that the COLA formula does not leave people behind," Benton said. "The people who depend on these benefits cannot afford another year of empty promises, inadequate adjustments, and shrinking purchasing power. They deserve more than a cost-of-living adjustment on paper; they deserve one that works in real life."

There's no telling when and if lawmakers will act to improve the COLA formula to account for real-time changes in the cost of living. However, there are ways retirees can maximize their benefits and protect their purchasing power.

Consider a high-yield account to earn interest: Consider keeping some or all of your Social Security payments in an interest-bearing account to earn interest on your payments. Many banks and credit unions are currently offering high-yield savings accounts and CDs that offer rates of up to 4%.

Look for ways to lower healthcare costs: Medicare's open enrollment period runs through Dec. 7. Use the Medicare Plan Finder tool to compare your coverage options during open enrollment, add your prescriptions and pharmacies for personalized drug-cost estimates, and see if you qualify for assistance with healthcare expenses.

Delay claiming your benefits to get the maximum benefit: You can start claiming your benefits as early as age 62; however, holding off on claiming your benefits until age 70 will allow you to collect a bigger monthly benefit. Claiming at 62 gives you access to money sooner but locks you into a smaller monthly benefit. At 67, you can claim 100% of your benefit. If you can afford to wait, claiming your benefits at age 70 generally boosts that amount to 124%.

Check spousal benefits: You may qualify for Social Security based on a spouse's or former spouse's earnings record. An ex-spouse can potentially qualify for spousal benefits if the marriage lasted at least 10 years and other eligibility requirements are met. If you're eligible for both your own retirement benefit and a spousal benefit, Social Security generally pays your own benefit first and adds a spousal benefit, if applicable, to bring your total up to the higher eligible amount.

articles.title: Netflix stock sinks after announcing Q3 earnings, Q4 revenue forecast falls short of estimates
articles.summary: Netflix stock fell after the streamer posted quarterly results.
articles.body:
Netflix ( NFLX ) stock fell 5% in after-hours trading on Tuesday as the streaming giant's Q4 revenue outlook came in below Wall Street estimates, signaling slower growth.

The company posted revenue of $12.87 billion in its fiscal third quarter, in line with analyst estimates. Earnings per share came in at $0.87, topping estimates of $0.82.

Fourth quarter outlook for the company's top line, though, came in at $13.44 billion, short of the consensus analyst expectation of $13.51 billion.

Wall Street has been laser-focused on the engagement metric , which accounts for how much time viewers spend watching and churn.

When it comes to the US, "our engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years," Greg Peters, co-CEO of Netflix, said during the earnings call.

"But we know that we can do better. And that's better for our upside. It's our goal to go from very good to great," he added.

Wall Street analysts were looking for signs on whether slowing engagement would bleed into the revenue growth numbers.

"That is exactly what we are seeing with the 4Q growth outlook," Geetha Ranganathan, senior media analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, told Yahoo Finance after the results were released.

"This kind of speaks to a slowing growth algorithm, which kind of spells trouble for the company without a doubt," she added.

The results follow the streaming giant's job-cutting plan and a leadership shake-up announced last week amid slowing viewer engagement.

Last week, former Disney executive Peter Rice was named Netflix's next chief content officer. Rice replaces Bela Bajaria, who worked at the streamer for nearly a decade and served as CCO since 2023.

Also last week, Netflix said it would cut 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, marking the company's largest reduction of employees since 2022.

The move comes as the company seeks to reinvigorate viewership growth and strengthen its content amid growing competition and short-form viewing habits.

Audiences have increasingly moved away from traditional television sets toward mobile devices, noted Piper Sandler director and senior research analyst Tom Champion in a recent interview.

"Where a lot of the [video] growth has come from has been short form, has been content especially built for mobile," Champion told Yahoo Finance. "That's given rise to TikTok and Instagram Reels, and increasingly, YouTube seems like the superpower in terms of video content."

Earlier this year, Paramount outbid Netflix for Warner Bros. Discovery and won shareholder approval for its revised $111 billion deal, including debt, in April.

articles.summary: By Sinéad Carew and Tharuniyaa Lakshmi Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Dow rose 1% on Tuesday, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500 while the healthcare sector provide...
articles.body:
Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Dow rose 1% on Tuesday, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500 while the healthcare sector provided Wall Street's biggest boost and technology was its biggest drag.

Healthcare led gains among the S&P 500's 11 major ‌sector indexes, hitting a record high. Eli Lilly was the S&P 500's biggest index point contributor while UnitedHealth, Merck & Co, Johnson & Johnson ‌and Amgen helped boost the blue-chip Dow industrials.

Declines in megacap stocks pulled down the communication services sector. Energy shares underperformed as oil prices fell after touching a five-month high. Oil ​traders were weighing a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan's army chief, a US-Iran mediator, against Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.

While the heavyweight technology sector eased 0.3%, it was the biggest index-point drag on the S&P 500 and kept the Nasdaq close to flat. Technology stocks had rebounded on Monday from a selloff last week when investors worried about steep spending and financing costs for AI developments.

"Equity ‌investors are still a little skeptical around the AI ⁠trade and the ability for some of these companies to monetize their investments, so you're seeing a bit of a rotation into other areas of the market," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, pointing ⁠to advances on Tuesday in small caps and healthcare companies.

"Investors are looking for other opportunities outside of tech, and healthcare is one of the beneficiaries of that," he said.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to 52,495.88, the S&P 500 gained 21.84 points, or 0.28%, to 7,712.57 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 6.07 ​points, ​or 0.02%, to 26,424.82.

The S&P 500 value index rose 0.9% compared with a 0.2% ​drop in its growth counterpart. The small-cap Russell 2000 index ‌finished up 1.7%.

With a 1% gain, the financial services sector was the S&P 500's second-biggest index point boost. Defensive sectors also outperformed, with real estate adding 1.7% and utilities climbing 1.2%.

A 1.7% drop in Netflix, a 1.6% decline in Meta and a 1% loss in Google parent Alphabet sent the communication services index down 0.9%.

articles.title: SpaceX quarterly revenue jumps, mostly from renting out data center capacity
articles.summary: Elon Musk‘s SpaceX posted a third-quarter profit that ​blew past estimates thanks to its surging AI business, sending its shares up 2.5% in extended trading.
articles.body: Elon Musk‘s SpaceX posted a third-quarter profit on Tuesday that ​blew past estimates as revenue more than doubled thanks to its surging AI business, sending its shares up 2.5% in extended trading. Capital expenses nearly tripled as ‌it invested in compute infrastructure. “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity and superintelligence,” Musk said on a call with investors. Starlink and SpaceX’s broader connectivity operations have been the company’s main financial engine, underpinning Musk’s AI ambitions. But SpaceX’s own AI software, including xAI’s Grok, has so far been overshadowed by rivals OpenAI, Anthropic and Alphabet’s Google. Revenue in the third quarter surged 161% to $14.58 billion for the three months ​ended September 30, compared with analysts’ estimate of $12.72 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. It reported a net income of $4.4 billion versus a net loss of $1.1 billion ​a year earlier and analysts’ expectation for a profit of $1.57 billion. On a per-share basis, it earned 45 cents according to IBES calculations, ⁠outstripping a 13-cent average estimate. AI revenue rose more than ninefold to $7.6 billion, mostly from renting out computing capacity, but AI took $16.4 billion of the company’s $19.6 billion in capital spending, which ​SpaceX expects to stay near that level in the near future. SpaceX is making its AI money mainly by renting out data center capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Google and Reflection AI rather ​than from its own models, a business closer to a cloud provider’s than an AI lab’s. “With AI revenue now the company’s biggest business line, the company’s hyperscale business is quickly providing operating strength and leverage which will carry into the advancements of its satellite and launch business. Increasingly the strength and diversification of SpaceX makes a merger with Tesla feel imminent,” said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech research group the Futurum ​Group. Barclays suggested last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting, with SpaceX the likelier acquirer, though neither company nor Musk has officially committed to favoring a ​deal. The company’s AI business spans Grok, social-media platform X and a fast-growing data center operation. It is also the company’s biggest area of investment. The business earns revenue from compute contracts with Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Reflection ‌AI. Operating losses ⁠at the AI unit have been large and SpaceX has cautioned it will need sustained investment before it can consistently generate profits. The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services. Starlink grows subscribers Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans. The ​company has said geographic expansion beyond the wealthiest ​countries could push average revenue per user ⁠lower over time. Investors have been keen to know whether that pricing pressure has started to show up as SpaceX enters more international markets and rolls out lower-priced plans. Investors are also watching whether SpaceX can keep growing while improving the economics of its network. It is spending heavily ​on coverage, capacity and direct-to-device mobile services. Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket system, has yet to enter commercial service. It is expected to enable ​deployment of higher-bandwidth Starlink ⁠satellites and orbital AI-computing infrastructure. The company’s ability to turn Starship into a reliably reusable vehicle is central to its longer-term strategy. Starship costs mount SpaceX successfully deployed several Starlink satellites last month, in Starship’s first orbital test flight that ended hours earlier than expected after an engine issue. The space segment includes commercial launches, government missions and Starship development and remains a significant source of costs and ⁠uncertainty. Falcon launch activity ​has stayed robust, but revenue can vary with the mix of internal Starlink deployments, commercial customer missions and ​government contracts. SpaceX has increasingly prioritized launches for its own satellite network over third-party payloads, while absorbing significant costs tied to Starship’s development.

articles.body:
How bond yields are slowing AI-fueled stock rally

Bond yields in the U.S. have risen this year, slowing down a stock market that has risen for years on the back of the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout.

After consistently rising, with a few exceptions, from late March through mid-August, the S&P 500 is down nearly 90 points from closing time on Oct. 7.

The Nasdaq composite, meanwhile, is down more than 1,100 points over the last two weeks, hitting its lowest point in more than a month on Tuesday.

The S&P 500’s information technology sector, which includes AI-focused firms such as Microsoft and Nvidia, is also down by more than 500 points from two weeks ago.

“If those [tech] stocks don’t do well, it’s pretty hard for the stock market to do much of anything,” Steve Sosnick , chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told The Hill.

Bond yields in the U.S. and globally have increased throughout the last seven months , as high oil prices amid the Iran war and mounting government deficits have compelled investors to flee the market.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield is down roughly 25 basis points from Oct. 7, when it reached a 24-year high of 5.365 percent during intraday trading.

But the note remains more than a full percentage point above where it stood at closing time on Feb. 27, the day before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran.

The 30-year Treasury bond yield has also declined over the last two weeks, falling from 5.733 percent during intraday trading on Oct. 8 to under 5.45 percent this week.
